learningObjective: Decide when a ResNet shortcut can remain an identity and when it must project the input so both branches have the same shape before addition.
mediumRationale: A deterministic two-panel SVG is the smallest medium that can align branch paths, tensor shapes, and the element-wise addition constraint. Contrasting one within-stage block with one stage transition makes the projection rule visible without duplicating the residual-gradient lesson owned by the related article.

mediumComparison.mermaid: Rejected: Mermaid can show a skip edge but cannot reliably align compact tensor-shape ledgers or make shape equality at the merge spatially precise.
mediumComparison.svg: Selected: deterministic SVG places both branch outputs beside the same plus operation and directly contrasts a free identity with a learned stride-2 projection.
mediumComparison.semanticHtml: Rejected: a comparison table could list input and output dimensions, but it would not reveal that both simultaneous branches must independently arrive at the same merge shape.
mediumComparison.interaction: Rejected: toggling stride or channels would add controls and hidden states when two fixed cases fully establish the invariant addition contract.
mediumComparison.paperReuse: Rejected: the original ResNet paper contains canonical block diagrams, but its arXiv availability does not establish a permissive adaptation license and its composition is unnecessary. No source figure, coordinates, typography, or layout is copied.
mediumComparison.noVisual: Rejected: the prose says to project when dimensions change but requires readers to mentally propagate height, width, and channels through two branches and diagnose why raw identity addition fails.

pages.insight: The preceding image-classification slide defines images as three-dimensional width-height-channel arrays, providing shape context but no network branching or addition.

The CNN slide has the deck's only direct ResNet section. It says skip connections ease gradient flow and enable deeper networks, but gives no residual-block diagram, bottleneck, tensor dimensions, or projection-shortcut rule.
The following Faster R-CNN slide names ResNet-101 as a feature-extractor option and shows backbone feature-map dimensions, but does not expose internal ResNet blocks or shortcut compatibility.
The next slide begins GANs, confirming the end of the local CNN and ResNet teaching sequence.

deckReview.notes: The complete 214-page local deck was text-indexed page by page for ResNet, residual, skip connection, shortcut, identity mapping, bottleneck, and projection. Transformer-related page 103 discusses residual connections only as generic architecture context and does not add the ResNet shape contract. No deck artwork, wording, data, or layout is reused.

sourceReview.notes: The hardest ResNet-specific mental model is not the generic skip edge but its shape contract. Element-wise addition requires equal height, width, and channels on both paths. The original example shows a within-stage 56 by 56 by 256 bottleneck reducing to 64 channels and restoring 256, followed by a schematic stage transition to 28 by 28 by 512. The latter uses a one-by-one stride-2 shortcut projection. Dimensions are consistent with the ResNet-50 stage pattern; the exact stride may be placed in a different main-path convolution in ResNet v1 versus v1.5, without changing the shortcut's required output shape.

agentReview.summary: Read the complete article, text-indexed all 214 deck pages, rendered and inspected pages 147-150, and checked the original ResNet paper, the pre-activation follow-up, official TorchVision documentation, and arXiv licensing guidance before selecting an original shortcut-shape comparison.

implementation.accessibility: The SVG has a linked title and detailed description. Every tensor shape is directly labelled; solid main paths, dashed shortcut paths, a crossed invalid identity, explicit valid labels, and separate identity and projection boxes encode the rule without color. Its 360-unit viewBox has no minimum width and scales at 390 CSS pixels; established theme variables preserve dark-mode contrast, and shared learning-figure print rules provide a light high-contrast rendering and prevent a page break inside the figure.
